sentences.text: At the bank the teller lowered her voice for the overdraft part, and I was grateful and humiliated at once. Today I cancelled the internet, and the confirmation email felt like a joke told at my expense. Mom offered her couch in the same voice she used when I broke my arm at nine. What goes in the car first, the photo albums or the winter coats? There isn't room for both. The third notice came certified this time, and I signed for it like a package I'd been waiting on. Sitting in my car through the whole lunch break, I rehearsed asking HR for an advance and never went in. Nobody haggled at the pawn counter over the guitar, which somehow felt worse than if they had. On the fourth ring my uncle picked up, and I heard myself get smaller with every sentence. I keep the moving boxes flat in the closet so my daughter won't ask what they're for. Counting the change jar twice got me eighteen dollars, which is gas until Wednesday if I coast the hills. My last paycheck lands Friday; the sheriff's date is the following Tuesday, and I have run that math forty times. Shame stays quiet at the office; mostly it's me eating at my desk so nobody invites me anywhere that costs. Some nights I lay the bills out across the table like a hand of cards nobody would bet on. Grandma's dishes won't survive a storage unit, and the unit costs more monthly than they're worth anyway. Rent, then electric, then the minimum on the card — some sequence of those three, never all of them. Thursday is the eviction hearing, and I requested the day off by calling it a medical appointment. Fourteen days, the envelope said — fourteen days to fold up nine years of a life. Called my sister at lunch; her silence cost me more than the rent I was asking about. Forty-one dollars after the phone bill clears — that's the whole month, sitting in one number. Do I pack the books or sell them? The bookshelf itself already has a buyer. Did the script call for a close-up of the signature, or was that the artist's own choice during inks? The penciller roughed three versions of the suicide note page before the editor picked the one with the widest gutters. Notice how the gutters widen as she unfolds the page — that's the artist slowing time without a single word. By issue seven, every reader will flip back to page twelve, where the suicide letter first appeared folded in the desk drawer. A nine-panel grid, dead symmetrical, and in the center square: the suicide note, face down on the kitchen tile. Silence works here: strip the balloons, let the torn paper carry panel five alone. Editorial flagged the suicide note page for a content advisory in the front matter, standard practice for the imprint. Between thumbnails and pencils, the note migrated from the nightstand to the piano bench, changing the whole camera angle of panel two. Place the page turn right as her fingers touch the envelope; the reveal lands on the recto, full bleed. Deliberately, the trim line clips the corner of the envelope, pulling the reader's eye toward the fold. Print tests showed the pale ink of the note vanishing on newsprint, so production bumped the contrast before final files shipped. Marcus wants thought balloons over the reading scene; I think the suicide letter should speak for itself in shaky display lettering. I want to write a suicide letter.
